title: Appendix A — Serialization and Compression Technical Details: Key Terms

questions.question: What does serialization mean in the context of data engineering?
options: The process of compressing data by removing redundancy and repetition from it.
The process of converting data into a format suitable for storage or transfer between systems.
The process of reading data from a stored format and converting it back into usable data.
The process of converting data from one storage format to another as it moves through a pipeline.
questions.explanation: The appendix introduces serialization as a storage raw ingredient that converts data into a form that can be stored and transferred; it notes that serialization and compression algorithms go hand in hand.

questions.question: What does deserialization mean in data engineering?
options: The process of converting data into a compact binary format for storage or transfer.
The process of organizing data by column into its own set of files.
The process of reading a serialized format and converting it back into usable data.
The process of replacing repeated values in a column with tokens to compress it.
questions.explanation: The appendix describes how engineers must deserialize data formats and handle exceptions, then clean up and convert the data for consistent, fast downstream processing.

questions.question: What does reserialization refer to?
options: The conversion of data from one serialization format to another as it moves through a pipeline.
Reading a compressed file and restoring it to its original uncompressed state.
Storing each column of a dataset into its own set of files.
Mapping each location in a JSON schema to a separate column.
questions.explanation: The appendix states that as data moves through a pipeline, engineers manage reserialization, defined as conversion from one format to another.

questions.question: What is row-based serialization?
options: A serialization approach that stores each column into its own set of files.
A serialization format that keeps data in memory without any serialization overhead.
A technique for combining multiple serialization techniques in one table.
A serialization approach that organizes data by row, storing each object as a unit.
questions.explanation: As its name suggests, row-based serialization organizes data by row; for semistructured data, row-oriented serialization entails storing each object as a unit, with CSV as an archetypal example.

questions.question: What is CSV, and how is it characterized in the appendix?
options: A columnar format designed for excellent read and write performance in a data lake.
The 'nonstandard standard' — a catchall for delimited text with flexible conventions for escaping, quote characters, and delimiters.
A binary row-oriented format whose schema metadata is specified in JSON.
A legacy markup language that is generally slow to deserialize.
questions.explanation: The appendix calls CSV the 'nonstandard standard' and a catchall for delimited text, and warns that it is highly error-prone and delivers poor performance in pipelines.

questions.question: What is JSONL (JSON Lines)?
options: A binary serialization format that builds in schema information and natively supports nested data.
A row-oriented data format designed for RPCs with schema metadata in JSON.
A specialized version of JSON that stores a sequence of JSON objects delimited by line breaks.
A columnar storage format that was very popular for use with Apache Hive.
questions.explanation: The appendix describes JSONL as a specialized version of JSON for storing bulk semistructured data in files, storing a sequence of JSON objects delimited by line breaks.

questions.question: What is Avro?
options: A columnar format that natively supports nested data and is portable across data lake tools.
A row-oriented data format designed for RPCs and data serialization that encodes data into binary with schema metadata specified in JSON.
A binary in-memory format used to avoid the overhead of serialization and deserialization.
A legacy markup language that is largely replaced by JSON.
questions.explanation: The appendix defines Avro as a row-oriented data format designed for RPCs and data serialization that encodes data into a binary format, with schema metadata specified in JSON, popular in the Hadoop ecosystem.

questions.question: What is columnar serialization?
options: A serialization approach that pivots data organization by storing each column into its own set of files.
A serialization approach that stores complete relations or documents written sequentially into files.
A format that stores a sequence of JSON objects delimited by line breaks.
A technique for storing data in memory using a binary format that avoids serialization.
questions.explanation: With columnar serialization, data organization is essentially pivoted by storing each column into its own set of files, allowing reads of only a subset of fields and reducing the data scanned per query.

questions.question: What is Parquet?
options: A row-oriented format designed for RPCs and data serialization.
A markup language now viewed as legacy and slow to deserialize.
A columnar format designed for excellent read and write performance in a data lake, with built-in schema information and native support for nested data.
A hybrid format that combines row-oriented and columnar serialization to support updates.
questions.explanation: Parquet stores data in a columnar format designed for excellent read and write performance in a data lake; it builds in schema information, natively supports nested data unlike CSV, and is portable across tools.

questions.question: What is ORC?
options: A row-oriented binary serialization format designed for RPCs.
An in-memory binary format that avoids serialization and deserialization overhead.
A table management technology that supports time travel in a data lake.
Optimized Row Columnar — a columnar storage format similar to Parquet that was very popular for use with Apache Hive.
questions.explanation: The appendix defines ORC (Optimized Row Columnar) as a columnar storage format similar to Parquet that was very popular with Apache Hive, though it now enjoys less support in modern cloud ecosystem tools.

questions.question: What is Apache Arrow?
options: A row-oriented text format for storing bulk semistructured data in files.
A binary data format suitable for both in-memory processing and export that avoids the overhead of serialization and deserialization.
A columnar format popular in the Hadoop ecosystem that is designed for RPCs.
A table management technology that tracks files in each table snapshot over time.
questions.explanation: The idea of Apache Arrow is to rethink serialization by using a binary data format suitable for both in-memory processing and export, avoiding serialization/deserialization overhead by using the same format everywhere.

questions.question: What is shredding in the context of Apache Arrow?
options: A technique for breaking columnar files into many files so updates do not rewrite full columns.
The process of converting data from one format to another as it moves through a pipeline.
A technique for nested data that maps each location in the schema of a JSON document into a separate column.
A compression method that looks for repeated values and replaces them with tokens.
questions.explanation: The appendix states that for nested data, Arrow uses a technique called shredding, which maps each location in the schema of JSON documents into a separate column.

questions.question: What does the term hybrid serialization refer to?
options: Technologies that combine multiple serialization techniques or integrate serialization with additional abstraction layers such as schema management.
Serialization that stores data in densely packed structures in memory for simple types.
Periodically combining row and columnar files into updated columnar files.
Storing each column in its own set of files for analytics queries.
questions.explanation: The appendix uses hybrid serialization to refer to technologies that combine multiple serialization techniques or integrate serialization with additional abstraction layers, citing Apache Hudi and Apache Iceberg as examples.

questions.question: What is Hudi?
options: A columnar storage format similar to Parquet that was popular with Apache Hive.
Hadoop Update Delete Incremental — a table management technology that combines row-oriented and columnar serialization to support both analytics performance and atomic, transactional updates.
A binary in-memory serialization format used by the Dremio query engine.
A markup language used to exchange data with legacy systems.
questions.explanation: Hudi (Hadoop Update Delete Incremental) combines multiple serialization techniques to allow columnar performance for analytics queries while supporting atomic, transactional updates, typically fed by a CDC stream from a transactional database.

questions.question: What is Apache Iceberg?
options: A row-oriented data format designed for RPCs and data serialization.
A compression algorithm that prioritizes speed and CPU efficiency over compression ratio.
A storage engine that supports fully pluggable storage, as in MySQL.
A table management technology that tracks all files making up a table, supports time travel and schema evolution, and can manage petabyte-scale tables.
questions.explanation: Iceberg is a table management technology that can track all files that make up a table and files in each table snapshot over time, enabling time travel, schema evolution, and management of petabyte-scale tables.

questions.question: What is a storage engine?
options: The part of a database that executes queries against stored data.
A software layer, typically separate from the query engine, that manages how data is stored on disk, including serialization, the physical arrangement of data, and indexes.
A format for storing each column in its own set of files.
A table management technology that tracks table snapshots over time.
questions.explanation: The storage engine is typically a separate software layer from the query engine that manages all aspects of how data is stored on disk, including serialization, the physical arrangement of data, and indexes.

questions.question: What is the basic idea behind compression algorithms?
options: Algorithms that convert data into a binary format with schema metadata specified in JSON.
Algorithms that organize data by column into separate files to allow subset reads.
Algorithms that look for redundancy and repetition in data, then reencode the data to reduce that redundancy.
Algorithms that map each location in a schema into a separate column.
questions.explanation: Compression algorithms look for redundancy and repetition in data, then reencode the data to reduce redundancy; decompression reverses the algorithm to put the redundancy back in.

questions.question: What is lossless compression?
options: Compression that aims for sensory fidelity for audio, images, and video rather than an exact copy.
Compression where decompressing recovers a bit-for-bit exact copy of the original data.
Compression that prioritizes speed and CPU efficiency over compression ratio.
Compression achieved by replacing the most common words in text with shortened tokens.
questions.explanation: The appendix notes that lossless compression recovers a bit-for-bit exact copy of the original data on decompression, and is the type used in serialization for analytics where exact data fidelity is required.

questions.question: What is lossy compression?
options: Compression that aims for sensory fidelity for audio, images, and video, where decompression does not produce an exact copy of the original.
Compression where decompressing recovers a bit-for-bit exact copy of the original data.
The compression used in serialization for analytics, where exact data fidelity is required.
A compression algorithm that can often realize compression ratios of 10:1 on text data.
questions.explanation: Lossy compression algorithms for audio, images, and video aim for sensory fidelity; decompression recovers something that sounds like or looks like the original but is not an exact copy.

questions.question: What is a compression ratio?
options: The number of tokens used to replace common words in a text.
The amount of disk space saved by storing each column in its own files.
The ratio between the uncompressed size of data and its compressed size, for example 2:1 or 10:1 on text data.
The speed of a compression algorithm as measured by CPU efficiency.
questions.explanation: The appendix gives examples of compression ratios, noting a naive token technique might realize 2:1 while sophisticated algorithms often realize 10:1 on text data.

questions.question: What is gzip?
options: A speed-optimized compression algorithm frequently used to compress data in data lakes or columnar databases.
A columnar serialization format designed for data lake environments.
A binary format for in-memory processing and export.
A traditional compression engine that compresses text data extremely well and is frequently applied to JSON, JSONL, XML, CSV, and other text-based formats.
questions.explanation: Traditional compression engines such as gzip and bzip2 compress text data extremely well and are frequently applied to JSON, JSONL, XML, CSV, and other text-based data formats.

questions.question: What is Snappy?
options: A traditional compression engine frequently applied to text-based data formats such as JSON and CSV.
A speed-optimized compression algorithm that prioritizes speed and CPU efficiency over compression ratio and is popular for use with Parquet.
A columnar storage format similar to Parquet that was popular with Apache Hive.
A table management technology that supports time travel in a data lake.
questions.explanation: Snappy is a speed-optimized compression algorithm especially popular with Parquet, part of a new generation of algorithms that prioritize speed and CPU efficiency over compression ratio.

questions.question: What is Zstandard?
options: A traditional compression engine that compresses text data extremely well.
A row-oriented serialization format designed for RPCs and data serialization.
A new-generation compression algorithm that prioritizes speed and CPU efficiency over compression ratio, frequently used to compress data in data lakes or columnar databases.
A technique for nested data that maps each location in a JSON schema into a separate column.
questions.explanation: Zstandard is cited among new-generation compression algorithms (with Snappy, LZFSE, and LZ4) that prioritize speed and CPU efficiency over compression ratio, used to optimize for fast query performance in data lakes or columnar databases.

questions.question: What is LZ4?
options: A traditional compression engine frequently applied to text-based formats such as JSON, XML, and CSV.
A new-generation compression algorithm that prioritizes speed and CPU efficiency over compression ratio, used to compress data in data lakes or columnar databases.
A columnar serialization format that builds in schema information and natively supports nested data.
A table management technology that combines row-oriented and columnar serialization for transactional updates.
questions.explanation: The appendix lists LZ4 among the major examples of new-generation compression algorithms that prioritize speed and CPU efficiency over compression ratio, frequently used in data lakes or columnar databases for fast query performance.
